title: What Skills Show Up Most in Data, AI, and ML Jobs?
text:
There are a lot of things someone interested in data or AI could spend time learning. Python and SQL are obvious examples, but there are also cloud platforms, databases, machine learning libraries, and newer tools related to LLMs.
Instead of looking at another list of “top skills,” I wanted to see what employers were actually mentioning in job posts.
My question was:
I used R and rvest to scrape the September 2026 Hacker News “Who is hiring?” thread.

title: What Skills Show Up Most in Data, AI, and ML Jobs?
text:
Getting the Data
The Hacker News thread works well for this because the job posts are available directly on the webpage and do not require a login.
I first downloaded the page and saved a copy of the HTML.

library(rvest)
library(here)
library(xml2)

hn_url <- "https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49522897"

page <- read_html(hn_url)

raw_html_file <- here(
  "data",
  "raw",
  "hn_who_is_hiring_sep2026.html"
)

xml2::write_html(
  page,
  raw_html_file
)

Saving the HTML was useful because I could keep working with the same version of the page instead of downloading it again every time I ran the code.
I then selected the comment rows from the page.

comment_rows <- page |>
  html_elements("tr.athing.comtr")

Hacker News includes both original job posts and replies underneath them. I used the comment indentation level to remove the replies and keep only the top-level posts.
After doing that, I had 261 hiring posts.
One thing to keep in mind is that one post can advertise more than one position. Because of that, I treat each company post as one observation rather than each individual job opening.

title: What Skills Show Up Most in Data, AI, and ML Jobs?
section: Finding Data, AI, and ML Jobs
text:
Finding Data, AI, and ML Jobs
My first idea was to search the entire job description for words such as “AI,” “data,” and “machine learning.” The problem is that this can include posts that are not actually hiring for those types of roles.
For example, a company could mention AI when describing its product but only be hiring a general software engineer.
To make the filter more specific, I only looked at the first 350 characters of each post. The beginning usually contains the company name and the positions being advertised.
I then searched that section for titles such as Data Scientist, Data Engineer, Data Analyst, Machine Learning Engineer, AI Engineer, and Research Scientist.

jobs_raw <- jobs_raw |>
  mutate(
    role_zone = str_sub(text, 1, 350)
  )

data_jobs <- jobs_raw |>
  filter(
    str_detect(
      role_zone,
      data_role_pattern
    )
  )

This left me with 39 Data, AI, or ML-related hiring posts out of the original 261.
The filtering was done automatically using the same rule for every post.

title: What Skills Show Up Most in Data, AI, and ML Jobs?
text:
Which Technologies Show Up Most?
For those posts, I searched the full text for a set of technologies such as Python, SQL, AWS, GCP, PostgreSQL, Docker, Kubernetes, PyTorch, and LLMs.
I counted each technology only once per post. So if one company mentioned Python several times, it still only counted as one Python observation.
Here is what I found:





Technologies mentioned most often in Data, AI, and ML-related Hacker News hiring posts.




Python stands out pretty clearly. It appeared in 19 of the 39 posts, or about 48.7%.
LLMs were second at about 35.9%.
GCP, PostgreSQL, and PyTorch each appeared in about 12.8% of the posts.
One result I did not expect was SQL. The exact word “SQL” only appeared in about 7.7% of the posts.
That does not mean SQL is unimportant. Some companies listed PostgreSQL or Snowflake instead of explicitly writing “SQL.” I kept them separate because I wanted the results to reflect what was actually written in the posts.

title: What Skills Show Up Most in Data, AI, and ML Jobs?
text:
What I Would Learn First
If I were using these results to decide what to study, Python would be the easiest place to start. It showed up in almost half of the relevant posts and can be used across data science, machine learning, and data engineering.
The number of LLM mentions also stood out to me. More than one-third of the posts mentioned LLM-related technology, which shows how common it has become in this particular group of tech companies.
After Python, I would probably focus on a mix of database and cloud skills rather than trying to learn every machine learning library at once. PostgreSQL, GCP, AWS, and Azure all appeared in the sample.
For someone more interested in AI and machine learning specifically, PyTorch and experience working with LLMs also seem useful based on these postings.

title: What Skills Show Up Most in Data, AI, and ML Jobs?
text:
Limitations
This is a fairly small sample. It only uses one month of Hacker News job posts, and Hacker News has a lot of startups and technology companies. The results should not be treated as a picture of the entire job market.
The posts also come from different countries, so this is not specifically a study of U.S. employers.
Another limitation is that a technology appearing in a post does not always mean it is required. Sometimes companies describe their current tech stack even when they are not asking applicants to already know every tool.
Finally, my filter depends on specific job titles. A relevant job with an unusual title could be missed.

title: What Skills Show Up Most in Data, AI, and ML Jobs?
text:
Takeaway
For this Hacker News sample, Python was by far the most commonly mentioned technology in Data, AI, and ML-related hiring posts. LLMs also appeared surprisingly often, while cloud platforms, databases, and machine learning tools showed up across a smaller share of posts.
The main thing I took from this is that looking directly at job postings can be more useful than relying on generic lists of “skills you need.” It gives a more concrete idea of what companies are actually mentioning right now.

title: What Does a p-Value Really Mean?
text:
One of the most common misunderstandings in statistics is the meaning of a p-value. Suppose a researcher runs a hypothesis test and obtains a p-value of 0.03. It is tempting to say that there is only a 3% chance that the null hypothesis is true. However, this interpretation is incorrect.
A p-value answers a different question.
Suppose the null hypothesis is denoted by (H_0). The p-value is the probability of observing a result at least as extreme as the one in our data, assuming that the null hypothesis is true. In simplified notation,
[ p = P( H_0). ]
The important part is the condition “(H_0) is true.” The p-value does not directly tell us
[ P(H_0 ), ]
which would be the probability that the null hypothesis is true after observing the data. These two probabilities may look similar, but they answer very different questions.

title: What Does a p-Value Really Mean?
text:
A Coin Example
Imagine that we want to determine whether a coin is fair. Our null hypothesis is
[ H_0: p = 0.5, ]
where (p) is the probability of getting heads.
Now suppose we flip the coin 20 times and observe 18 heads. If the coin is actually fair, the probability of getting 18 or more heads is only about 0.02%.
That makes 18 heads look very unusual under the assumption that the coin is fair.
The p-value captures exactly this idea. It asks:

If the coin really were fair, how likely would it be to observe a result this extreme or even more extreme?

If we are doing a two-sided test, we would also count outcomes that are equally extreme in the opposite direction, such as getting 2 or fewer heads.
A very small p-value therefore suggests that the observed data are difficult to reconcile with the null hypothesis.
However, even a very small p-value does not prove that the null hypothesis is false. It only tells us that the data would be unusual if the null hypothesis were true.

title: What Does a p-Value Really Mean?
section: What a p-Value Does Not Mean

title: What Does a p-Value Really Mean?
text:
What Does 0.05 Mean?
A common convention is to call a result “statistically significant” when the p-value is below 0.05. This cutoff is useful as a rule of thumb, but it is not a magical boundary between truth and falsehood.
A p-value of 0.049 and a p-value of 0.051 represent almost the same amount of evidence, even though one may be labeled statistically significant and the other may not.
This is why researchers should not focus only on whether a p-value crosses the 0.05 threshold. Effect sizes, confidence intervals, sample size, and the economic meaning of the result also matter.

title: What Does a p-Value Really Mean?
text:
Why the Concept Feels Unintuitive
The p-value is easy to misunderstand because people naturally want to ask:

“Given the data, how likely is my hypothesis to be true?”

But the p-value asks the reverse question:

“Assuming my hypothesis is true, how unusual are these data?”

That reversal in conditioning is the main reason the concept is unintuitive.

title: What Does a p-Value Really Mean?
text:
The Main Takeaway
The easiest way to remember the meaning of a p-value is:

A p-value measures how surprising the data are under the null hypothesis.

It does not measure the probability that the null hypothesis itself is true.
A p-value is therefore one piece of evidence about how well the data fit a hypothesis, not a direct probability that the hypothesis is right or wrong.
